Ex-Twitter CEO Parag Agrawal says AI agents currently use the web at only 10% to 20% of human levels. His company, Parallel Web Systems, is now valued at $2B after raising $230M to build search for the next 5,000x to 10,000x of agent traffic.

Most people will read this as a story about search. I read it as a story about SME underwriting.

SME credit has always been an information problem. Many small businesses have thin files: short financial history, unaudited statements, little bureau data. They do have a web footprint, though. It shows up in company registries, official gazettes, public procurement awards, customer reviews, hiring activity and local news.

Until now, collecting that evidence meant an analyst with 20 browser tabs open. That is why so many lenders simply skip small tickets: the review costs almost as much as the margin. An agent with a proper retrieval layer changes the economics:

* Taktile’s CEO says its banking customers already run complex KYB checks with Parallel in minutes instead of hours.
* Parallel’s Basis framework attaches citations and a calibrated confidence score to every extracted field. That is exactly what a credit committee and a regulator will ask for.
* The Monitor API turns underwriting from a one-time snapshot into continuous surveillance after disbursement: a new lawsuit, a key executive leaving, a lost public contract, a sanctions hit.
* Parallel’s own example prices enrichment of a 2,400-account list at $0.01 per task, against $0.12 with a default search provider. These are vendor numbers, but a 12x gap matters for a portfolio of $20k loans.

In SME lending, the model is rarely the bottleneck. The evidence is.

Three limits I still see:

* Coverage is uneven. A family bakery has a fraction of the digital footprint of a SaaS startup, so the agent can quietly penalize the less “online” borrower.
* The web is adversarial. Agrawal himself talks about prompt injection and agent-generated SEO. Once applicants learn what the agent reads, they will start writing it.
* Explainability. “The agent found it” is not a reason code. Every feature needs its source, timestamp and confidence logged before it touches a decision.

Agents will not replace the SME scorecard, they will feed it, monitor it, and shrink the manual review queue that makes small business loans so expensive to originate.

If you lend to SMEs, which open-web signal would you trust first in an underwriting decision?

The most important number in Legora’s $8.8 billion funding round isn’t $8.8 billion.

It’s 40%.

Last week, Legora announced another $550 million investment, valuing the legal AI company at $8.8 billion.

But buried in the announcement was a more interesting detail.

In-house legal teams accounted for over 40% of Legora’s new customers last quarter.

Just a year ago, they represented only a small fraction.

I think this signals something potentially much bigger than another successful LegalTech company.

For decades, law firms and corporate legal departments have purchased software for fundamentally different reasons.

Law firms invest in technology to deliver services more efficiently and profitably.

Corporate legal departments invest in technology to manage legal work, control costs and reduce their dependence on external providers.

The same AI technology can strengthen both sides of that relationship. But their economic incentives are very different.

When AI makes research, document review, contract analysis and drafting substantially more accessible, corporate legal teams may be able to handle more work internally.

Not necessarily by hiring more lawyers.

But by increasing the capacity of the teams they already have.

That could fundamentally change the economics of external legal services.

More work handled in-house. More selective use of outside counsel. Greater pressure on fees for repeatable work.

Of course, this doesn’t eliminate the need for law firms. Complex litigation, specialist advice and high-stakes transactions will continue to demand external expertise.

And growth in AI adoption doesn’t automatically prove that legal spending is shifting.

But having worked with both corporate legal departments and law firms across the world, I think the direction is worth watching closely.

Legal AI may be unusual: its success with one customer segment could fundamentally change the economics of another.

Which raises an interesting question:

When both the buyer and seller of professional services gain access to the same AI, who captures the productivity dividend?

Your SAP system holds your most sensitive data. Now you’re adding AI on top of it.

Employee records. Customer master data. Financial transactions. Pricing. Supplier contracts.

When Joule, embedded Business AI and custom models on SAP BTP start touching that data, three questions matter more than any demo:
1️⃣ Is it responsible? Is it fair, explainable and under human control?
2️⃣ Is it governed? Who owns it, who approved it, and who is monitoring it?
3️⃣ Is it private? Is personal data minimised, masked, retained only as long as needed, and kept out of prompts and logs?

I put together a practical guide that brings all three together. A few takeaways:
✅ Tier every AI use case by risk before you build or switch it on. A forecasting model and a candidate-ranking model should not go through the same gate.
✅ Make privacy by design a gate, not a checkbox. Run a DPIA for high-risk use cases and mask personal data before it reaches any model.
✅ Use what SAP already gives you. Authorisations, Read Access Logging, UI masking and ILM-based retention and blocking are your foundation.
✅ Don’t let AI bypass authorisations. Assistants running on privileged technical users can show people data they should never see. Carry the user’s identity through retrieval.
✅ Remember the hidden copies. AI logs, caches, embeddings and vector stores also hold personal data, and need retention and deletion rules too.
✅ Never copy unmasked production data into test. It’s still one of the most common sources of privacy incidents.
✅ Keep humans accountable. Decisions about hiring, pay or discipline should never be left to AI alone.

The guide also covers a governance operating model, RACI, KPIs, an AI incident playbook, a 12-month roadmap and ready-to-use checklists.

Why the World Turned Pessimistic on AI

60% of US workers believe AI will eliminate more jobs than it creates. Through June 2026, AI was cited in over 101,000 job cuts — nearly double all of 2025. For four consecutive months, AI was the number-one reason employers gave for layoffs.

This is not a mood. It is the dominant measurable sentiment across every major worker survey in developed economies.

The pessimism-optimism split does not track culture. It tracks replacement exposure. Rich-country economies run on knowledge work — exactly the labor AI substitutes most directly. A senior analyst earning $300K for pattern repetition disguised as judgment is more replaceable than an office cleaner whose work requires physical presence.

Poor-country economies run on agriculture and physical labor. AI adds tools without displacing structures. A farmer with AI crop forecasting becomes more productive, not unemployed. The optimism in the Global South is not naivety — it is an accurate threat assessment by people whose jobs cannot be performed by a language model.

The math is self-defeating. Meta cut 8,000 employees while spending tens of billions on AI. Oracle eliminated 25,000 positions. 99% of CEOs expect AI-driven layoffs by 2028. US consumer sentiment hit 44.7 — the lowest since 1951.

When you replace workers to cut costs, you are cutting your own customers. Henry Ford understood this a century ago. The AI industry is running Ford's logic in reverse.

The industry defaulted to replacement without ever consciously choosing it. CEOs have only seen AI do execution-layer tasks: write faster, code faster, generate faster. Faster is a replacement metric. The alternative — precision amplification of human judgment — is invisible to people who have never operated at the judgment layer.

The two paths produce opposite outcomes. Replacement is a death spiral: eliminate workers, workers stop buying, market contracts. Amplification is a flywheel: one person produces 20x output, the company grows, each new hire gets amplified, more growth leads to more hiring.

Every worker wants to become 20x more valuable. Every employer wants 20x output from the same team. Every government wants GDP growth without displacement. The alignment is obvious. The industry chose the opposite.

The pessimists are right about the threat. They are wrong to assume there is only one version of the future.

If your resume stops a year ago, a hiring manager has already asked the question before you walk in the room:

"What have you been doing since?"

Some comments on my last post have stayed with me.

One person has been job searching for more than a year.
Another lost their job during COVID and is still fighting their way back.
Many of you stepped away to care for someone you love.

I get it. None of those reasons are anything to be ashamed of.

But a blank space doesn't tell your story. It lets the reader make one up.

So give them something real to read instead. Any of these beats a resume that just stops:

→ Continued education. A certification, an online course, or a new skill like Excel, QuickBooks, Salesforce, or AI tools. It shows you kept growing.

→ Volunteer work. Treasurer for a nonprofit, event coordinator for your church, operations help for a local charity. Real responsibilities count as real experience.

→ Contract or freelance work. Consulting, side projects, or helping a former colleague's business. Give it a title, dates, and results, just like any other job.

→ Temp or part-time work. Even a few hours a week gives you a current role, current skills, and current references.

→ Family caregiving. "Family Caregiver, 2024–2026" is a legitimate entry. Coordinating with doctors, managing schedules, handling insurance, and running a household budget take serious organizational skill, so list them the way you would for any role.

A few more things that make a real difference:

A COVID layoff needs no apology. "Position eliminated  COVID-19 restructuring" says everything it needs to. What matters now is what came after, so fill those years with anything from the list above.

If you've been searching for a year or more, start something this week. A course you begin this month or a contract role you pick up next month gives your resume a current entry right away. It's not too late. It's never too late.

Look at contract-to-hire roles. Staffing firms place people in temporary positions that often turn permanent. It's one of the fastest routes back in.

Tell your story with confidence. "My role was eliminated and my family needed me. I've used this time to [X], and now I'm ready for [Y]." That's a complete answer. No over-explaining, no apology.

A long search or a season of caregiving says nothing about your worth.

Your resume just needs to show that you kept moving.

Tanjong Pagar hawker centre, 7: 50pm. Dinnerrush over, chicken rice going cold.

Wei Ling stirred her rice without eating it. Farhan, two years ahead of her in the same firm, watched for a while.

"Eat lah. Cold already."

"Can't. Stomach is tight." She laughed, but it came out thin. "Last night, 11:40pm, still checking a client report. The AI wrote forty pages in four minutes. Four minutes, Farhan. Checking it took me six hours."

"Because you check properly."

"Because if one number is wrong, it's my name on the sign-off. Not the AI's. Not the vendor's. Mine." Her voice dropped. "My manager said, 'Just review quickly, the AI is 90% accurate already.' So which 10% do I get blamed for?"

Farhan put down his chopsticks. "Last quarter, my team's output tripled. Headcount stayed the same. Nobody asked who is reading all of it."

"Everyone says human oversight is so important." She shook her head. "In meetings, it's a big word. In real life, it's me, alone, at midnight, scared. Hiring freeze also, so no juniors coming in. I'm the junior. I'm the safety net."

A long pause. A tray clattered somewhere behind them.

"Sometimes in the MRT," she said quietly, "I think about just resigning. No plan. Just stop. Then I feel guilty, because my parents think this job is a good job. Everyone says I should be grateful to still have one."

"Grateful and exhausted can be true at the same time."

Her eyes went red. She looked at the ceiling fan, blinking hard. "I used to like this work, you know. Now I open my laptop and my chest goes tight."

Farhan did not rush to fix it. He slid the barley drink toward her.

"Can tell you something? Two weeks ago, I almost sent a wrong contract clause to a client. The AI wrote it so confidently. I caught it at the last minute. Went to the toilet after and my hands were shaking. Never told anyone."

She stared at him. "You too?"

"Everyone is too. Nobody says it, because saying it sounds like you cannot cope." He leaned in. "But maybe this is not a coping problem. Maybe it is a design problem. Who owns the review? How many hours are we given for it? Why is the junior holding the risk?"

"Cannot just ask like that."

"Then ask together. Three of us, one email. Not 'AI is too much.' Just: name an owner, count the review hours, no blame when we flag a mistake."

Wei Ling finally picked up her chopsticks. Ate one slow mouthful.

"If they say no?"

"Then at least we know what kind of company it is. And you decide with a clear head, not a 11:40pm head."

She nodded, wiped her eyes with a napkin, and laughed properly this time. "Aiyoh. Cry in hawker centre. Very Singapore."

"Next time kopi is on me."

The person catching the AI's mistakes is often the most junior, the most scared, and the least protected. 

Oversight only works as a competitive moat if the humans doing it are resourced, trained, and safe to speak up.

Recruiters are nervous about their jobs. It's the biggest challenge I see to AI transformation in hiring. There's denial about what is happening, and plenty of turfism. What can or should humans do, and what could be left to agents?
I think the problem stems from the way the discussion has been framed: AI is going to take away jobs, and some of those jobs are going to be recruiters.
AI is not going to take any job. Not today, not tomorrow. Agents were not designed to do jobs. Thinking in terms of jobs is yesterday's thinking.
What agents are coming for is your work. Stop thinking of jobs and start thinking of workflows. This might sound like semantics, but I see it as critical to understanding the relevance of people working in hiring. Organisations exist to produce products or services people will pay for.
Companies organised the work needed to produce these outputs into jobs behind a pyramid-shaped organisational chart. Boss at the top, minions at the bottom. It is a system that worked reasonably well, with recruiters responsible for hiring people to fit the boxes denoted by each job title.
Fast forward to today and AI sees us shuffling the deck, which means a rethink. I don't think jobs are a relevant way to organise companies anymore. Workflows are. Work backwards from company outputs. For hiring, map every input between a requirement being raised and somebody arriving for their first day.
I have measured around 84 inputs on average to make a hire, plus work around the funnel: attracting people, screening, selecting, progressing or mostly dispositioning them. This is work in a workflow. Agents are not coming for your jobs, they are coming for your work. If what stays with you does not have a value equal to your salary, you are probably toast.
We also need to decide how much responsibility and autonomy to hand over. There is very little in a hiring funnel we could not give to agents, from job creation to hire, with a new starter as the outcome. The question is not what we could do, but what we should do. Design the hiring workflow from scratch, with agents doing everything.
Then identify which steps require decision making. Those won't need a human to do the work, but will need one to supervise and review the decisions. This work is human.
Next, consider which steps don't require a human, but would be better performed by one. We are discovering people are far more likely to meet commitments, like turning up for interviews, made to other humans than those made to machines. The social contract keeps this work safe.
That same social contract is proving critical for vacancy take-on. Humans are proving better than agents at scoping out requirements and getting commitments from hiring managers. This lays the foundation for the workflow. If you can excel at the human in the loop bits and get diligent at review, it's time to start looking at what new human work you can add to your own workflow.
That's how you stay safe.
Peace Out,
Bill

→ A record of every decision and outcome that no agent can quietly rewrite
